tier_reason: chapter_10/benches/multiply.rs (Criterion) times matrix_multiply, aliased to simd.rs's matrix_multiply_simd under --features nightly and to matrix_multiply_unsafe_indexing otherwise, so the comparison code is public; the 359 to 208 microsecond figures are the book's own run relayed by the lead, with no CPU, exact compiler version or results in the repo, so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Criterion 0.5.1 (Cargo.lock) via cargo bench, which inherits the release profile ([profile.release] debug = true in chapter_10/Cargo.toml, opt-level otherwise default); the repo README asks for Rust 1.82.0 or newer and a nightly toolchain for the SIMD step (cargo +nightly bench --features nightly, portable_simd); no rust-toolchain.toml, no .cargo/config.toml, no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu, and no exact compiler version recorded.
corrections.workload: 100x100 f32 Vec<Vec<f32>> matrix multiply (random inputs from make_random), Criterion benchmark via cargo +nightly bench --features nightly: scalar get_unchecked loop versus a 4-lane std::simd f32x4 dot product (row slice load, column gathered by four scalar loads) with a horizontal swizzle-add; inputs cloned inside the timed closure.
corrections.caveats: Code check: simd.rs loops p in steps of 4 and skips any tail (if p + 4 <= a_cols), so a shared dimension that is not a multiple of four silently drops terms and returns a wrong product (all zeros when a_cols < 4); the speedup holds only for the multiple-of-four case the benchmark uses. The b column is gathered with four scalar get_unchecked loads from four separate row Vecs per step (no transpose or packing), and the gain over the scalar loop comes largely from four independent partial sums breaking the scalar reduction's dependency chain (the summation order, and so the rounding, differs from the scalar versions). Per the README's run commands the SIMD step runs under cargo +nightly while the scalar baseline runs under the default toolchain, so the two figures may differ in compiler version as well as code, and they are separate runs. Baseline is the book's own scalar Rust, not an optimized library. The repo carries the code for this step (chapter_10/src/lib.rs, chapter_10/src/simd.rs, Criterion bench chapter_10/benches/multiply.rs; Cargo.lock pins criterion 0.5.1 and rand 0.8.5) but no benchmark results, no CPU and no compiler version; the quoted timings come only from the book text as paraphrased in the lead and appear on no page opened here, so they are first-party and unverified. The bench times only the alias matrix_multiply (the unsafe-indexing version on a default build; the SIMD version with --features nightly), and its closure clones both 100x100 input matrices, allocates the Vec<Vec<f32>> result and drops all three matrices inside the timed region, which dilutes every step; reproducing the earlier steps needs editing the alias in lib.rs. A second harness, chapter_10/src/bin/cli.rs, times one matrix_multiply call with elapsed::measure_time (a single run, no warm-up) and writes a flame graph; which harness produced the book's figures is not stated in the repo. All steps compare Rust against its own earlier Rust version; no BLAS, ndarray, nalgebra or C++ baseline appears anywhere in the repo (none of the blas-lapack baselines OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS), so baseline_in_list is false (derived: 2*100^3 flops in 208 microseconds is about 9.6 GFLOPS, in 2.24 ms about 0.9 GFLOPS). Safety: the unchecked versions never validate dimensions, so ragged rows or a b with fewer than a_cols rows is undefined behavior instead of a panic. The repo has only 3 commits, 11 stars, and no tests that check the results.

notes: Code matches the lead (simd.rs, lib.rs alias, Criterion bench); book figures not checked (book not consulted per harness), kept at C per the wave11/wave12 book-record precedent. Off-baseline for blas-lapack (own scalar loop only), tail-dropping correctness bug and unchecked-index UB on bad dimensions are shortcomings to record; metadata (MIT, 11 stars, 3 commits, last commit 2026-03-13) confirmed.
